title: Light: The Fastest Thing There Is
subtitle: How light races, bounces, bends and paints the world
subject: Physics

p: Flick a light switch and the room is bright before you can blink. That is because light moves at about 300,000 kilometres every second. In one second a beam of light could race around the whole Earth seven and a half times. The fastest jet ever built would need more than 5 hours to go around once.

Why is light so fast? Light has no weight at all. A heavy ball takes a big push to get going fast. Light has no weight to hold it back. It simply goes as fast as anything in the universe can go. Scientists call this the cosmic speed limit.
pages.cap: Light leaving the Sun takes 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach your face.
pages.fact: Did you know? Light could cross Canada from coast to coast in about one fiftieth of a second.

p: Because light takes time to travel, you never see things as they are now. You see them as they were when the light left them. Moonlight is 1.3 seconds old. Sunlight is 8 minutes old. If the Sun went out, you would not know for 8 minutes.

The nearest star after the Sun is called Proxima Centauri. Its light takes 4.2 years to reach us. The Andromeda galaxy is so far away that its light takes 2.5 million years. When you look at it, you are seeing light that started its journey before modern humans existed. A telescope is really a time machine.
pages.cap: The light from the Andromeda galaxy left home 2.5 million years ago.
pages.fact: Did you know? Some stars you see at night may have already burned out, but their old light is still arriving.

pages.h: Every look at the sky is a look back in time
p: Starlight is a message that took years, centuries or millions of years to arrive. The night sky is the oldest picture you will ever see.

Some things make their own light. The Sun, a candle flame, a light bulb, lightning and a firefly are all light sources. Most of them make light because they are hot. A candle flame is about 1,000 degrees Celsius. The surface of the Sun is about 5,500 degrees. Hotter things glow brighter and whiter.

Most things do not make light. The Moon looks bright, but it is just a grey rock bouncing sunlight back to us. Your book, your hand and your dog are the same. You can see them only because light from somewhere else hits them and bounces into your eyes. Turn off every light source and they all disappear.
pages.cap: A candle makes light because its flame is hot enough to glow.
pages.fact: Did you know? A firefly makes light with a chemical reaction, not heat. Its glow is cool to the touch.

p: Light does not turn corners on its own. It travels in perfectly straight lines. That is why shadows exist. When you stand in the Sun, your body blocks some light rays. Behind you is a patch of ground the rays could not reach. That dark patch is your shadow, and it has your shape.

Shadows change through the day because the Sun moves across the sky. When the Sun is low in the morning, a 1 metre stick throws a shadow about 1.7 metres long. At noon in summer, with the Sun high in the sky, the same stick has a shadow shorter than itself. Ancient people used this to build the first clocks.
pages.cap: A low Sun makes a long shadow. A high Sun makes a short one.

pages.q: How long does light from the Sun take to reach Earth?
pages.why: The Sun is 150 million kilometres away, and at 300,000 kilometres per second light needs about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to cover that.

p: When light hits something, some of it bounces off. This is called reflection. A mirror is so smooth that every ray bounces off at the same angle it came in. If a ray hits at 30 degrees, it leaves at 30 degrees. That is why a mirror gives a clear, sharp picture.

A wall or a piece of paper looks smooth, but under a microscope it is bumpy like a mountain range. Light rays hit the bumps and scatter in every direction. That is why you can see a page from anywhere in the room, but you cannot see your face in it. A lake on a calm day is a mirror. Add a breeze and it turns into a blur.
pages.cap: Light bounces off a mirror the same way sound bounces off a wall to make an echo.
pages.fact: Did you know? A good mirror reflects about 95 percent of the light that hits it.

p: Stand in front of a mirror and raise your right hand. Your reflection raises the hand on your right side too, but it looks like its left hand. People say mirrors flip left and right. They do not. A mirror flips front and back. The person in the mirror is facing you, so what is forward for you is backward for them.

The reflection also seems to be as far behind the glass as you are in front of it. Stand 1 metre from a mirror and your twin looks 2 metres away. This is why the word AMBULANCE is printed backwards on the front of the vehicle. In a driver's mirror it reads the right way round.
pages.cap: A mirror makes a matching copy, like the two halves of a butterfly.

p: Watch a shadow move and you are watching the Earth turn.
steps: On a sunny morning, stand a pencil upright in a lump of modelling clay on a sheet of paper outside.
Every hour, draw a line along the pencil's shadow and write the time at the end.
Measure each shadow with a ruler. Which hour has the longest shadow? Which has the shortest?
The next sunny day, use your drawing to tell the time without a clock.
pages.cap: Your pencil shadow swings like the hand of a slow clock.
pages.safe: Never look straight at the Sun, even for a moment.

p: Put a straw in a glass of water and look from the side. The straw looks bent or broken at the surface. The straw is fine. The light is bending. This is called refraction. Light travels at 300,000 kilometres per second in air, but only about 225,000 in water and 200,000 in glass.

Why does slowing down make light turn? Imagine a toy cart rolling off a smooth floor onto thick carpet at an angle. The wheel that hits the carpet first slows down, so the cart swings toward that side. Light does the same thing when it enters water. Because of this, a stone on the bottom of a pool looks closer to the surface than it really is.
pages.cap: A stone under water looks higher up than it really is because the light bends on its way out.
pages.fact: Did you know? Spear fishers aim below where the fish seems to be, because refraction lifts the picture.

p: A lens is a piece of curved glass or plastic. Because it is curved, it bends light rays by different amounts, so they meet at one point. A lens that bulges outward in the middle is called convex. It can gather sunlight into a hot bright dot, or make small things look big. A simple magnifying glass makes letters look about 3 times larger.

A telescope uses lenses to gather light from faint, far-away things and bring it to your eye. In 1609 Galileo pointed one at the Moon and saw mountains for the first time. Eyeglasses, cameras, microscopes and your phone all use lenses. So does your own eye.
pages.cap: Galileo's telescope made the Moon look about 20 times closer.

pages.q: Why does a straw in a glass of water look bent?
opts: The water pushes the straw sideways
Light changes direction when it moves from water into air
The glass is curved like a lens
pages.why: Light slows down in water and speeds up in air. That change of speed makes the rays turn, so the straw's picture arrives at your eye from a different place.

p: In 1666 a young scientist named Isaac Newton let a thin beam of sunlight into a dark room and put a glass prism in its path. On the far wall, a stripe of colours appeared: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet. He had split white light apart.

Why does a prism do this? Every colour of light bends by a slightly different amount when it enters glass. Violet bends the most and red bends the least, so they fan out. Newton then used a second prism to squeeze the colours back together, and out came plain white light again. White is not the absence of colour. It is every colour at once.
pages.cap: A prism fans white light out into seven colours because each colour bends by a different amount.
pages.fact: Did you know? Newton chose seven colours to match the seven notes of a musical scale. Many people can only clearly see six.

p: A rainbow needs two things: the Sun behind you and rain in front of you. Every raindrop is a tiny round prism. Sunlight enters the drop, bends, bounces off the back wall, bends again on the way out and splits into colours. Millions of drops do this together, and you see a glowing arc.

The colours always leave the drops at an angle of about 42 degrees from the sunlight. That is why every rainbow has the same curve and the same size. A rainbow is really a full circle, but the ground cuts off the bottom half. From an airplane, with rain below, people sometimes see the whole ring.
pages.cap: Sun behind you, rain in front, and millions of tiny prisms make an arc.
pages.fact: Did you know? Nobody can walk to the end of a rainbow. When you move, the rainbow moves with you.

pages.h: White light is every colour at once
p: Sunlight looks plain, but hidden inside are all the colours of the rainbow. A prism, a raindrop or a soap bubble can pull them apart.

pages.h: Try it: make a rainbow indoors
p: You can split sunlight with a glass of water.
steps: Fill a clear glass almost to the top with water.
Place it on a sunny windowsill so the Sun shines through it.
Put a sheet of white paper on the floor where the light lands. Move the paper slowly until you see a stripe of colours.
Try again with a small mirror in the water, tilted toward the ceiling. Where do the colours appear now?
pages.cap: A glass of water bends sunlight just like a prism.
pages.safe: Do not look at the Sun or at its reflection in the mirror.

pages.h: Why a red apple is red
p: Things do not have colour on their own. They have colour because of the light they bounce back. White light hits a red apple. The apple's skin soaks up the blue, green and yellow light and reflects only the red. The red reaches your eyes, so you see a red apple. Under a blue light the same apple looks almost black, because there is no red light to bounce.

A white shirt reflects all the colours. A black shirt soaks up nearly all of them. Soaking up light means soaking up energy, which turns into heat. On a sunny day a black car roof can be 20 degrees hotter than a white one. That is why light clothes feel cooler in summer.
pages.cap: Dark colours soak up light and turn it into heat.

p: Sunlight is white, so why is the sky blue? Air is made of tiny molecules far smaller than a wave of light. When sunlight passes through, these molecules knock blue light around in every direction much more than red light. Blue bounces all over the sky, so wherever you look, blue light arrives. On the Moon there is no air, so the daytime sky there is black.

At sunset, sunlight comes in sideways and travels through almost 40 times more air than at noon. Nearly all the blue is scattered away before it reaches you. What is left is orange and red. That is why sunsets glow.
pages.cap: At the edge of day, sunlight crosses so much air that only the reds get through.
pages.fact: Did you know? On Mars the dust makes the daytime sky butterscotch and the sunsets blue.

pages.q: What colour would the daytime sky be if Earth had no air?
pages.why: Blue sky comes from air molecules scattering blue light. With no air there is nothing to scatter, so the sky is black even in full daylight, just like on the Moon.

p: Light enters your eye through a small black hole called the pupil. Behind it sits a soft, clear lens. The lens bends the light and focuses it onto the back wall of your eye, the retina. The picture that lands there is upside down. Your brain flips it the right way up without you ever noticing.

The retina is covered with about 126 million light sensors. When light hits them, they fire tiny electric signals along the optic nerve to your brain. The whole trip takes about one tenth of a second. Your brain turns millions of signals into one picture. You are not really seeing with your eyes. You are seeing with your brain.
pages.cap: Signals from your eye race along nerves to your brain in a fraction of a second.
pages.fact: Did you know? Your eye lens changes shape in a fraction of a second to focus near or far.

pages.h: Seeing in colour and in the dark
p: Your retina has two kinds of sensors. About 6 million cones see colour, but only in good light. There are three types: one tuned to red, one to green and one to blue. Your brain mixes their signals to make every colour you know. About 120 million rods see in dim light, but only in shades of grey. That is why colours fade at night.

In bright sun your pupil shrinks to about 2 millimetres. In the dark it opens to 8 millimetres, letting in 16 times more light. Your rods also need time to wake up. After 20 to 30 minutes in darkness you can see about 10,000 times better than when you first stepped in.
pages.cap: In the deep sea there is almost no light, so animals make their own.
pages.fact: Did you know? A cat's eye has a mirror behind the retina. Light gets a second chance, so cats see well in the dark and their eyes shine in a torch beam.

p: The rainbow is only a thin slice of all the light there is. Light is a wave, and the colour depends on the length of the wave. Red waves are about 700 nanometres long and violet about 400. A nanometre is a millionth of a millimetre. Your eyes see only this range.

Longer waves are called infrared. You feel them as heat from a fire. Even longer waves are radio and microwaves. Shorter waves than violet are ultraviolet, which gives you sunburn. Shorter still are X-rays that pass through your body. Bees can see ultraviolet, so flowers show them patterns we miss. Some snakes sense infrared and can hunt a warm mouse in total darkness.
pages.cap: To a bee, many flowers have glowing ultraviolet landing stripes that point to the nectar.

p: Light carries energy. You can feel it when sunshine warms your skin. At noon on a clear day, about 1,000 watts of sunlight fall on every square metre of ground. That is like ten bright old-fashioned bulbs shining on a patch the size of a door. Plants catch this energy to make food. Solar panels catch it to make electricity.

Scientists spent 300 years arguing whether light is a wave or a stream of tiny particles. Today we know it is both at once. The particles are called photons. In 1905 Albert Einstein explained how a photon can knock an electron out of metal. That idea is how every solar panel works.
pages.cap: A solar panel turns photons into a flow of electricity that can light a bulb.
pages.fact: Did you know? Enough sunlight hits Earth in one hour to power the whole world for a year.

pages.q: Which colour of light bends the most when it passes through a prism?
pages.why: Violet has the shortest waves we can see, and short waves bend the most in glass. Red has the longest waves and bends the least, so it ends up at the other edge of the rainbow.

p: Right now, most of the internet is travelling as flashes of light. Thin glass threads called optical fibres, each thinner than a hair, run under streets and across oceans. A laser at one end blinks billions of times a second. Each blink is a one, each gap is a zero. The light bounces along inside the glass at about 200,000 kilometres per second.

Why glass and not copper wire? Light does not get tired. A flash can travel 100 kilometres through fibre before it needs a boost. Electric signals in copper fade after about 100 metres. One fibre can carry millions of video calls at the same time. A single cable under the Atlantic Ocean holds up to a few dozen of them.
pages.cap: Every letter you send becomes a burst of ones and zeros, flashed through glass as light.
pages.fact: Did you know? About 99 percent of the data crossing oceans travels through undersea fibre cables, not satellites.

p: For 100 years, bulbs made light by heating a thin wire until it glowed white hot, about 2,500 degrees Celsius. It worked, but only 5 percent of the electricity became light. The other 95 percent became heat. Touch an old bulb and you will burn your finger.

A modern LED makes light a different way. Electricity pushes electrons through a tiny crystal, and they give off photons directly, without the heat. An LED uses about 85 percent less electricity than an old bulb for the same brightness, and lasts about 25 times longer. The best light maker of all is still the firefly. Nearly all of its energy becomes light, and almost none becomes heat.
pages.cap: An old bulb glows because its wire is white hot. An LED glows cool.

p: No. As far as we know, nothing in the universe can move faster than light. Why not? The faster something with weight goes, the harder it gets to push. Near the speed of light it would need endless energy to go any faster. Only things with no weight at all, like light, can reach the limit.

Humans are not close. The fastest machine ever built is the Parker Solar Probe, which skims past the Sun at about 690,000 kilometres per hour. That sounds huge, but light is 1,500 times faster. At the probe's speed, a trip to the nearest star would take about 6,500 years. Light does it in 4.2.
pages.cap: Even our fastest spacecraft would need thousands of years to reach the nearest star. Light needs four.
pages.fact: Did you know? If you could travel near the speed of light, time would pass more slowly for you than for your friends at home.
